subject: gnomeTinkerer
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: gnome tinkerer with a backpack of gadgets.
Style: whimsical low-poly mix.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a full module for a gnome tinkerer character, aiming for a solid humanoid skeleton structure covering hips, spine, chest, neck, head, jaw, arms with shoulder/elbow/wrist/finger joints, and legs with hip/knee articulation, while keeping the implementation efficient at a few hundred lines.

I'm fleshing out the character design: a pointy red hat, white beard, big nose, goggles pushed up on the forehead, a leather apron, and a backpack loaded with gears, a telescope, pipes, a glowing lantern, a spring, wrench, and gauge, drawing on clockwork and glow kits for the metallic and glowing effects. I'm working out precise height proportions for the hips, torso, neck, and head to keep the gnome's exaggerated big-head proportions balanced against its roughly 1.1m total height, and I'm now defining the joint hierarchy and spine chain using a catmull curve through hip and shoulder positions.

Setting up joint parenting...

I'll keep the lower jaw mostly hidden under the beard, attaching the beard shapes to the head bone as rigid elements along with a small mustache. For the head itself, I'm shaping it as a sphere-like skull with specific scale and position values centered around HC.

For the eyes I'm weighing two approaches: projecting a custom eye decal (white sclera, brown iris, highlight) onto the faceted skull surface, versus building separate eyeball parts (white sphere plus pupil) embedded into the head. Decals are riskier on a coarse 12x9 segment sphere, so I'm leaning toward actual geometric eye parts to reduce uncertainty.

For the eyes I'll go with white spheres, big irises, black pupils, highlights, and thick lids. Then bushy white eyebrows as spikes, a big round red-pink nose sphere, rosy cheek spheres, and pointed ears made as sideways cones. For the beard, I'm thinking a layered mass built from extruded blade shapes sweeping down from the lower face to the chest.

Rather than lathing, I'll build the beard from overlapping tapered cone shapes rooted along the jawline, longer in the center, shaded white with grey undertones, plus a flattened core sphere at the chin to anchor everything. Setting up rows of these cones at different heights and lengths to create natural layering...

Settling on 5 sides for the facets. Now for the hat, I'll build a tall floppy cone using a bezier sweep curving backward with a tapered radius so it caps to a point at the tip, bending the path from the base up and back for that drooping witch-hat look.

Adding a lathed brim ring, a red mottled hat band with a gold buckle and star patches, plus goggles on the front made from brass lathe rings with lens cylinders.

I'm shaping the hat brim as a lathed ring sitting just above the brow, checking its radius and height so it doesn't overlap the eyes while still reading as a proper brim.

Now I'm building the cone of the gnome hat with a bending bezier path that tapers from a wide base down to a thin tip, drooping slightly like a floppy nightcap rather than standing straight up.

Still working out the belly shape...

Now I'm picking a color palette: red-orange hat, teal tunic, brown leather apron, plum-grey trousers, tan gloves, brass-buckled brown boots, and a leather backpack. I'm also sketching the arm placement, starting the shoulder joint path for a catmull curve.

Setting up the skeletal chains for the arms in an A-pose, defining shoulder-elbow-wrist joints with slight outward bend, then planning simplified finger chains (three fingers plus a thumb per hand, each with a single joint) for the hands.

Planning a hand helper to build four digits per hand (index, middle, ring, thumb) as base-to-tip capsule chains, keeping the rest pose with arms angled down-forward and fingers extended and spread.

Still placing hand geometry...

Setting the torus cuff with proper axis orientation, then laying out the leg chain with hip, knee, and ankle joints, plus a separate toe joint attached as a child of the ankle tip.

For the boots, I need a shape with a flat bottom so feet sit properly on the floor plane -- trying a scaled sphere first but realizing the poles won't give a flat surface, so I'll switch to a lathe geometry instead.

Still shaping the boot geometry...

Fine, legs rest slightly apart with no IK needed. Now I'm working out the hip and torso geometry, placing the pelvis and leg joints so the sweep radii blend smoothly without cutting through the arms, then adding a wide leather belt with a brass buckle looped around the waist.

Still working out the sweep parameters...

Fitting a flat apron onto a curved belly creates a gap, so instead of stacking slabs I could use a decal approach — projecting an SVG apron design onto the torso surface so it naturally conforms to the curve. This lets me add pockets, rivets, stitching, and a gear emblem as texture detail rather than separate geometry, sitting just slightly off the surface.

I'm also reworking the torso itself as a single loft so the belly bulge is built into the body shape, shifting station centers forward at the belly and chest while keeping hips and shoulders aligned, then tying the loft to the spine chain rooted at the hips joint.

I'll skip the sides option since it's unclear if loft supports it, risking it being ignored rather than throwing an error. Then I'm adding an apron decal onto the torso loft, positioned at the front with a defined direction and size.

For the back, I'm placing a bulky leather pack with gadgets using a box shape sized roughly 0.3 wide, 0.36 tall, 0.18 deep, positioned behind the torso near the chest bone. For the straps, I'm sweeping curved paths over the shoulders connecting the pack to the front of the torso, using catmull-rom points to drape the strap geometry naturally over the shoulder curve.

Now I'm detailing the hero gadgets on the backpack itself, starting with a lathed brass telescope tube strapped to the side angled upward, and a flat or solid gear train mounted on the back face of the pack.

Working out gear train module and tooth counts...

I'm finding the gear placement pokes outside the pack boundary with these dimensions, so I'm trying smaller modules to shrink the gears and keep the vertical span within the 0.36 limit, recalculating each gear's pitch, outer radius, and distance from center accordingly.

I'm checking that gears g1 and g2 placed at diverging angles (up vs. down) don't overlap, then adding further child gears g3 and g4 on different axle layers with small shifts to avoid collision, verifying clearance between layers and confirming mesh distances stay consistent with each gear's module and tooth count.

Then I'm working through positioning the gear train relative to the chest bone, making sure axle direction, joint orientation, and gear thickness defaults are consistent with the rest of the model's structure.

For the hanging lantern, I want a small cylinder with a cage and a glowing yellow-orange core, suspended from a hook on the pack's left side via a thin chain with a ring attachment. I'm also considering where to place a pressure gauge, leaning toward mounting it on the pack's left face using a decal-style texture.

For the gauge itself I'll use a rim cylinder with a textured circle facing outward. Then I want to add a whimsical copper chimney pipe emerging from the pack's top right, with small flat low-poly smoke puffs in white-grey, plus tools like a wrench and hammer tucked into a loop, flat-textured cogs, and a rolled blueprint scroll tied with a red ribbon on top of the pack.

I'm also thinking of adding a small spinning brass propeller on top, an antenna with a glowing crystal bulb, a telescope on the side, a lantern, a coil, buckled side pouches, and maybe a bedroll -- building out the full tinkerer aesthetic. Hands stay in rest pose so no held tool, but I'll add a tool belt with pouches and a hammer loop, star-decal patches on the hat, and a big curling white mustache sweeping over the mouth using catmull curves.

For the mouth, I'm hiding it mostly under the beard and mustache but still giving it a proper jaw structure -- a small lower jaw bone with pink lip boxes for upper and lower lip, leaving just a tiny peek of a smile visible. The beard itself I'll rig to the head bone rather than the jaw for simplicity, hanging long and static.

Now I'm working out head geometry: placing the skull sphere, figuring eye positions using surface azimuth/elevation hits relative to the head center, and sizing/positioning the nose as a slightly stretched sphere just below eye level.

Still placing facial features... working out rosy cheek spheres and then building pointed ears using an extruded leaf-shaped outline (rather than a simple spike) so they flatten properly, mirrored for left/right using the sign multiplier.

Now I'm setting a warm pink-tan base skin tone with subtle mottled texture, then shaping the eyebrows as bushy white sweeps using tapered capsules angled from inner to outer brow positions, tucked under the hat brim.

I'm adjusting vertical positions so the eyebrows, eyes, and hat don't collide — raising the hat base, lowering the eyes and brows slightly, and checking that head height and hat cone radius stay proportional. I'm also deciding to keep the hat centered with a slight backward lean, then placing goggles on the hat band near the front of the cone.

Still working out goggle placement, strap geometry, and the hat's bent bezier path points...

Now I'm figuring out the sweep shape with a faceted low-poly cross section, and planning the paint texture with darker red stripes and a stitched patch detail for the hat.

For the material I'll blend a lighter red top with darker red underside using countershade plus subtle mottling for a hand-painted look. I'm also placing a small gold sphere bell at the tip of the hat's path with slight sag toward the character's head.

I'm deciding to keep the hat tip rigid rather than rigging it with a floppy joint chain, since the role system doesn't cleanly support that kind of accessory animation. For the beard, I'll go with cream-white using a directional grain texture along the length of each strand, rendered as painted cones.

Working through the beard's placement now: the core sphere sits low on the jaw beneath the mustache and nose so it doesn't overlap the face mesh, and I'm calculating cone rows that sweep along the jawline from roughly -80° to 80° to build the individual beard strands.

I'm layering three to four rows of tapering cones at decreasing radii and lengths, around 30 faceted pieces total, to give the beard a jagged, bladed texture, then adding a few tufts of hair peeking out from under the hat.

Now I'm setting up the SDK calls: creating the builder, defining the hip joint, and building a spine chain through four catmull points that creates three spans named spine1, spine2, and chest, parented to the hips with a spine role assigned.

I'm placing the chest joint, then adding the neck and head joints with specific positions and directions, accounting for the gnome's short neck hidden by the beard and the skull's radius and center placement. I'm also adding a jaw joint parented to the head with its own orientation.

Now I'm building out the arms: setting shoulder positions relative to torso width, adding a sleeve puff sphere at the shoulder for the shirt, then constructing an arm chain using a catmull-rom path through shoulder, elbow, and wrist points with named joints for rigging.

Then I'm sweeping the arm geometry with a tapering radius profile, applying shirt color along the sleeve and adding a separate glove for the hand, plus a cuff ring at the wrist to mark the sleeve boundary.

Now I'm defining a palm sphere for the hand and planning the finger chains—thinking through how many joints each finger needs and designing a helper function to build each finger as a short polyline of joints with its own radius.

Setting finger segment sizes, then attaching each hand's finger chain to the wrist tip joint of the arm. Now building leg chains parented to hips with hip/knee/ankle joints per side.

Still shaping leg geometry...

Adding the toe joint for digit movement, then placing foot parts: a sole cylinder anchored near the ankle bone and a toe cap sphere on the toe joint, checking their vertical alignment makes sense.

Now I'm shaping the heel and footprint with a stretched elliptical cylinder, adding a separate darker sole piece and a toe-cap sphere scaled for a rounded foot silhouette, plus small boot buckle details like a brass strap buckle. For the torso I'm considering playful extras like puffed shoulder sleeves and maybe a scarf around the neck for character.

I'm scrapping the scarf idea and instead focusing on a dark leather belt with a brass buckle and three small pouch boxes placed around it, which needs to sit correctly on the torso surface derived from the loft/sweep geometry. I'm working out how the surface-loop query picks the right contour at a given height so the belt wraps around the torso rather than accidentally grabbing an arm loop, since arms are separate meshes and shouldn't interfere with the torso surface sampling.

Now I'm figuring out the belt's cross-section orientation along its closed horizontal path, trying to determine whether the sweep's binormal ends up vertical or radial so I can pick the right rx/ry values to make it look like a tall, properly-thick belt rather than a thin rope.

Then I'm turning to the backpack: positioning its box behind the torso, choosing overall dimensions, and planning to build it from a main body with a mottled leather paint texture plus a separate flap/lid piece attached near the top.

For straps and buckles I'm using small boxes with brass accents, and I like the idea of applying a riveted panel treatment with dark seam ink to give the leather a stitched, hardware-studded look. I'm also marking a spot on the pack's back face to place a gear element with its own axis and tooth thickness.

Now I'm checking the pack's placement and sizing it up as the hero feature—making it larger with position roughly centered on the back, checking that its top edge, the lid, and the hips don't collide with the head, hat, or beard geometry, and confirming the hat's curled tip clears the pack behind it.

Next I'm adding the lid as a darker box on top plus front flap, then wrapping straps around the pack with brass buckles on the sides. For the side-mounted gear I'm planning the layout: a pressure gauge and lantern on one side, and a telescope plus tools on the other.

I'm also adding a bedroll, striped and tied, across the bottom of the pack, plus a blueprint scroll, propeller, antenna crystal, and steam pipe on top, with a gear train on the back. For the telescope itself, I'm defining a helper that builds tapered brass tube segments with ring bands using lathed cylinder sections.

Writing telescope dimensions...

Now I'm planning the propeller assembly on top of the lid, with a mast rod, hub, and two blades attached via a hinge joint.

I'm placing a glowing cyan octahedron crystal rod above the lid, scaled taller for emphasis, plus checking other glow spots like lantern and lenses. Then I'm adding a copper steam pipe leaving the lid, curved upward via a swept path with a funnel cone at the end.

Now I'm layering three whimsical puff spheres in pale grey-white tones rising above the pipe in increasing size, carefully positioning them to avoid clashing with the hat tip. I'm also working out where to fit a blueprint scroll cylinder, repositioning it away from the propeller to avoid overlap, settling on tucking it along the pack's lower back.

Lid top sits at y=.84 with items placed there. For the -X side I'm planning a wrench and hammer as loops — the wrench built from an extruded outline with a handle rod and a jawed head notch.

Still writing wrench outline...

Now placing the hammer next, with a wooden handle rod positioned vertically toward the back and a steel head box near the top, checking for overlap with other tools nearby.

I'm checking leg and arm positions to avoid clutter near the hip, then settling on placing the gauge upper-front and hammer mid-rear on the +X side, with the lantern hanging on a short chain lower-front — double-checking its hook height and chain length don't collide with the nearby hand position.

Now I'm adding belt pouches using raycasts against the skin mesh to find placement points, sizing small boxes with flaps, and sketching screwdrivers with colored handles poking out of them. I'm also planning an apron texture drawn as SVG — a bib shape in brown leather with stitched outlines and a central chest pocket decorated with tool icons like screwdriver handles and pliers.

Writing apron SVG decal...

I'm also working out how to position the decal reliably: writing a helper that casts a ray forward onto the torso and falls back to a nearest-point lookup so the apron always anchors correctly even if the direct ray misses.

I'm trying a short leather flap extruding down from the belt over the thighs, but checking the z-depth against the torso and leg radii shows it sticks out too far from the body.

Positioning the apron so it hangs like a skirt with the leather material, placing it just below the belt line. Now I'm planning the texture list: eye, apron decal, gauge, hat patch, and considering a gear emblem or "TINKER" text decal on the pack, while skipping extras like smoke cards or beard hair tufts for now.

Still expanding the texture plan to include a star-and-gear hat patch, a blueprint scroll texture wrapped around a cylinder, and a "GNOME & CO" label decal on the pack lid, plus glow effects for the lantern core, goggle lenses, and crystal, with leather rendered as a panelled brown grain.

Now I'm setting up the module imports, pulling in builder utilities, clockwork kit helpers like gear trains and metal paints, and the glow kit, then sketching helper functions for vectors and spheres to construct the gnome's body parts.

For the sphere-building helper, I'm weighing whether to pass a non-uniform scale array through the part options or bake the scaling directly into the geometry itself, since geometry.scale should correctly handle normal transformation for the flat-shaded parts.

Now I'm sketching out small utility functions: a `ball` helper for scaled spheres, a `box` helper that aligns orientation along an optional direction, and a `cyl` helper for cylinders positioned by center and direction. Then I'm starting to define the color palette, mixing mottled skin tones with countershaded hat colors.

Still writing palette colors...

I'm sketching out the skull as a flattened sphere part with skin surface, planning how eyes get placed via decals positioned around the head.

Writing eye SVG...

Still drawing the eye pupil and highlights...

Now I'm thinking about adding a small decorative star patch on the hat, designing it as a separate rounded square texture with a dashed yellow border and red star center, then decaling it onto the hat's cone surface.

For the hat band, I'm checking the lathe profile dimensions to make sure the band ring sits properly around the cone, catching that the band's inner radius needs to be smaller than the cone's taper at that height or it'll overlap awkwardly.

Now I'm working out the brim shape, lathing a flat disc-like profile that extends outward from the hat base with a slight curve up at the tip and down near the center.

I check that the brim at .2 radius extends past the face, dipping low enough to shade the eyebrows but staying clear of the eyes below, and consider shrinking it to .17 for better readability. I also note the lathe will use the default 12 segments for a low-poly look, then move on to positioning the goggles on the band at the front of the hat.

Still writing goggle geometry...

I'll place the bell slightly offset below the hat tip, checking it stays within the cap's radius. Skipping the stitched seam detail, keeping the hat droop simple, and adding pink inner ears with sideburn hair before moving on to torso coloring and ear extrusion details.

I notice the ear shape collides with the brim, so I'm lowering the ear angle and adjusting its outline points so the tip sits below the brim's edge, then setting up the nose as a small sphere positioned on the face.

Now I'm computing where the skull surface sits at the nose's height to figure out how far the nose protrudes — giving it a fairly prominent, gnome-like bump between where the eyes will sit. With that placed, I'm starting the mustache geometry as a curved sweep beneath the nose.

Checking the skull depth at mouth height, then positioning the mustache tips so they poke out past the surface, followed by a small pink lip shape on the jaw that peeks through beneath the mustache, with a separate beard mass starting lower on the chin.

The beard cones extend down toward the chest, reaching y .55-.56 where the torso front sits near z .15, so the beard naturally drapes over the apron bib area, which actually looks good layered on top of that decal.

Now I'm sketching remaining details: hair tufts, brows, shoulder pads, and sleeve puffs near the shoulder joint. Then I'm moving to the arms and hands in A-pose, computing wrist and palm positions before building out the glove/finger geometry.

Writing finger and thumb joint positions...

Still building finger chains...

For the torso, I'm layering shorts starting at hips and a shirt loft covering down to the hem, making sure clothing pieces stack correctly.

Moving the hem loop to y .4 to avoid rim-narrowing issues, and deciding to skip a collar trim since the plane would awkwardly cut through the shoulder and arm shapes. I'm thinking about adding suspender straps with brass buckles on the chest as an extra detail over the torso.

I'm sketching the strap curve as a drape path with points running from shoulder down to chest, then checking how the loft's rounded end caps will affect the top station height — worried the cap radius could push the torso top too far up and swallow the neck/head area, so I'm adjusting the end width/height values to keep the top around .78-.79 instead.

For the bottom I want a flat cap rather than round, since a round bottom would bulge below the tunic hem into the legs — so I'm setting caps to flat at start and round at end, moving the hem station to y .37, and defining intermediate stations at .46, .55, .62, and .66 with varying widths/heights and slight forward z-offsets to give a potbelly curve before the shoulder dome at the top.

Now I'm working out the shoulder strap geometry, placing points that sweep from the back near x .085 up over the dome at the top of the shoulder and down to the front, relying on nearest-surface mapping to handle the curve, then adding a thin leather strap sweep with a small brass slider box at the end.

I'm also sketching a brass buckle positioned where the strap meets the chest, using a nearest-point lookup to anchor it to skin, and checking that the pack's strap attaches correctly where the rear strap end at z -.13 meets the pack front at -.15. I want to confirm the surface and loft API details—whether torso surfaces stay valid after pose changes, and whether a bone argument can mix a chain and a joint like hips and spine—before deciding to skip a neck sphere since the beard will cover that seam anyway.

Now I'm building a gear train for the gnome's pack mechanism, defining several gears with varying teeth counts, spokes, bores, and tinted metal colors like verdigris copper and gilt, then verifying the spoke and rim clearances for each gear to make sure the hub and rim dimensions leave enough margin given the module size.

I'm checking that gear 3 sits concentric with gear 1 but shifted outward along the axis, confirming its overlap with gear 0 is fine because they're on different depth layers, and then adding a fourth meshing gear with ten teeth branching off gear 3 at an angle.

I'm now computing coordinates for this fourth gear relative to gear 3's position and direction, verifying it stays within the overall pack width, and checking it doesn't collide with gear 2 since both their planar distance and layer depth keep them separated.

Moving on, I'll design a helper function for connecting rod segments between arbors with specified radii and colors. Then I'm planning the lantern hanging from a hook on the pack's right side: a brass cap, a thin-rod cage frame, and a glowing yellow-orange glass core at its center.

Now I'm positioning the lantern body and its chain link from the hook down to the cap, followed by placing the pressure gauge on the pack face with its gilt rim and textured dial, working out the orientation so the gauge face reads correctly when viewed from the front.

On the +X side I'm adding a hammer with a wooden handle rod and a steel head box, plus brown strap rings, spacing it apart from the lantern and gauge so nothing overlaps along that face. Then I'm switching to the -X side, laying out a telescope with an angled base and multi-section length, and placing a wrench near the pack's edge below it.

I'm also deciding where to add a coil spring detail, settling on tucking it beneath the gear cluster between the pack's bottom and the bedroll, using a thin blued-steel helix swept along a short horizontal line, then positioning the bedroll itself just below that as a rolled cylinder near the pack's base.

For the bedroll I'm building a thin cylinder rotated onto the horizontal axis, giving it a striped canvas texture with a warm rust-and-cream pattern, and wrapping a couple of torus straps around it to hold it closed. I'm also considering skipping an extra side pouch and instead thinking about adding a small brass plate or label somewhere on the pack's lid as a decorative touch.

I'm placing a small "TINKER & SONS" tag as a plane on the back of the pack lid, figuring out its position and orientation so it faces outward correctly, and also planning a blueprint-style SVG texture wrapped around a cylinder for a scroll detail, plus simple flat-colored sphere puffs and some grain texture on the beard cones using a position-based paint pattern.

For the beard itself I'm using a spike helper to generate low-poly cone blades along normalized directions from the head, with five-sided cones colored for the beard. I'm also figuring out eyebrow placement using small capsules, computing their y/z coordinates relative to the skull front so they sit naturally under the brim without being hidden by it.

Now I'm adjusting the overall layout, shifting eyes to y .865 and brows between .9 and .933, then raising the hat brim and band so they clear the brow geometry while keeping the goggles higher at y .98 and the cone base tucked just inside the head at y .94.

For the hat itself, I'm defining a tapered cone path through a few control points with shrinking radius toward the tip, using faceted 8-sided geometry for a stylized look, and applying the same faceted treatment to the beard cones. I'm considering small decorative touches like a stitched band, a feather, or a tiny pin to add whimsy without overcomplicating the shape.

Simplifying to a small brass gear ornament placed on the hat band instead, skipping the feather idea and freckle details. Ready to move on to writing the actual code now.

Writing vector helper functions...

Still writing skeleton hierarchy...

Finishing the torso loft with shirt coloring and cap settings, then double-checking whether the loft function actually supports flat/round cap options.

Now I'm positioning a belt loop around the belly at its widest point, layering it over the apron decal, and adding a buckle as a small box geometry stuck to the front.

Then I'm placing two pouches on either side of the torso front by raycasting onto the surface and sticking small boxes at those hit points.

Next I'm adding a flap and rivet detail on the apron, then setting up an SVG decal for the apron graphic sized proportionally to match the torso dimensions, sketching out the bib outline path.

Writing SVG code...

Adding a large stitched lower pocket with brass rivets at the corners, plus dark oil stain ellipses near the bottom, while deciding the beard covering the upper bib means I can skip extra decal text there.

Now I'm moving to the backpack: building a boxy main body attached at the chest bone, painting it with paneled sections, and adding a chamfered lid on top along with wrap-around straps and small brass buckle details on the sides.

I'm working out the vertical placement of the straps to avoid clashing with the gear outlines, checking clearances near the lower gear bottom around y=.417 and fitting an upper strap near y=.74 just below the lid, verifying it clears the gear tops at .652-.7225.

Now I'm positioning the gear train's z-depth on the back face, nudging it to around -.37 to -.40 so the layered gears embed properly without poking through, then considering small brass details like corner caps and buckle clasps but deciding to skip some for simplicity.

I'm sketching the lid's scroll decoration as a cylinder placed near the top center, checking its radius and position against the lid surface and the head geometry behind it to avoid overlap.

Now I'm figuring out the propeller assembly: a mast rod rising from the lid top to a small hub, with blades extruded outward along x and angled slightly, attached via a hinge joint named "prop" with its own bone. I'm also placing an antenna rod with a glowing crystal tip and a brass ring, then starting to plan a copper pipe sweep while checking its x-position doesn't collide with the antenna.

Now I'm defining the copper pipe's curved path with collar rings, and building a funnel shape at the end using a lathe profile instead of a simple open cylinder so it reads as a proper bell-mouth. I'm orienting the funnel along the tangent direction of the path's endpoint so it points outward rather than straight up, and planning small rising puffs to emit from the funnel's mouth.

I'm also thinking through the remaining accessories (lantern, crystal, goggles) and smaller details like elbow patches and cuffs, sanity-checking the total part count and overall figure height so proportions stay reasonable. Then I move into the jaw and lip geometry -- a lower jaw box hidden under the mustache/beard, bound to the jaw bone, and a small ball for the upper lip positioned under the nose on the head bone.

Next I'm placing cheek spheres colored a soft pink tone positioned against the skull front, then adding small hair tuft cones behind the ears tucked under the hat brim. After finalizing positions I shift to writing the arm sweep geometry with tapering radii and color bands splitting the sleeve into shirt fabric and a leather bracer section near the wrist.

For accents, I'm adding a brass cuff ring torus along the forearm using a chain point's position and tangent direction to orient it correctly, sized to match the arm's radius at that point, then planning a similar cuff detail for the boots lower on the legs.

With the body loop structured to handle left/right symmetry for limb decorations, I'm also setting up a decal patch on the hat using a surface ray cast to find the attachment point and orienting the texture along the correct axis.

Now I'm finalizing imports, deciding which utilities like rng and noise functions I'll actually need versus leaving them out to keep things clean, and planning the SVG assets—an eye shape, apron, patch, brass tag with engraved text, blueprint scroll, and gauge dial.

Writing beard blade placement logic...

Still computing beard geometry rows...

Checking row-1 cone placement against the mouth region—the first row sits near the lips at that y-position, so I need to verify the beard cones don't overlap the lip geometry there.

I'm adjusting the cone positions downward to .745 so the mustache and lips stay above the beard rows, keeping a visible gap between them. Then I'm spacing successive rows at .71, .675, .65, .63 with increasing lengths so the beard tapers down toward the hips.

For the mustache itself, I'm using a smooth catmull sweep with tapering radii attached to the head bone, and planning the brow as a capsule shape and other features as lathes bound explicitly to the head bone. For the ears, I'm considering skipping an inner pink decal and just keeping a single skin-colored extrude shape for simplicity.

Now I'm working out the inner ear detail by scaling the outline smaller with slightly less thickness so it protrudes symmetrically on both faces, then moving on to assembling everything together and writing the leg joint hierarchy parented to the hips with a chain sweep defining the leg points.

Defining leg chain code...

Adding toe joint attached to leg tip, then shaping the foot sole as a scaled cylinder for the boot.

Adding the brass buckle box near the ankle, then I'll compile everything into actual code and double-check the part function's color parameter types.

Still writing component code...

Still placing lantern parts... adding a hook ring and chain linking it to the pack, double-checking the hammer's z-offset doesn't clash with the lantern, then moving on to positioning the telescope's base.

Building the telescope with tapered brass and copper sections, each with its own radius and material, computed along a direction vector from a base point, plus a lens cap ring and leather grip wrapped around one segment.

Now hammer needs a rod and head, checking bone attachment through chest. For the TAG decal I'm placing a plane facing backward near the lid, verifying the texture reads correctly from the viewer's perspective and positioning it just in front of the lid's back face.

I'm also checking the pack's seam defaults, confirming loop structures for rows, and verifying the torso surface loft works with the bones. I want to double-check the lathe outline constraint on the first point's x-coordinate, make sure arm and wrist bone roles are accounted for, and confirm which helper functions like noise, paint, mix, and smoothstep are actually used before finalizing the code, possibly adding a custom shirt paint with a lighter belly and dirt near the bottom.

Writing paint shader logic...

Still writing helper functions...
